newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian church leaders call for Christmas harmony.
newsitem.headline: Australian church leaders call for Christmas harmony.

text.p: Australian church leaders on Wednesday called for racial harmony and compassion at Christmas, warning self-interest, greed and racism were threatening the nation's stability.

In a message ahead of next week's Christian festival, Sydney's Catholic archbishop Cardinal Edward Clancy warned that the harmony of Australia's multi-cultural society, which consists of 69 ethnic groups, remained fragile.

"Our aboriginal brothers and sisters are still grossly disadvantaged, East Timorese and other refugees are denied elementary compassion, and ill-conceived controversy threatens the stability of our multi-cultural family," Clancy said.
"Jesus Christ came into our world offering salvation, unity and peace. He made himself the brother of us all...irrespective of race, colour or culture...," he said.
"May this Christmas witness a re-commitment on the part of us all to that unity in diversity seeded long ago in a stable in Bethlehem."
Australia's 300,000-odd Aborigines continue to be the most disadvantaged group in the 18 million population, with a life expectancy 10 to 15 years shorter than non-indigenous people.

Asian boatpeople are kept in desert detention centres, some for more than a year, awaiting the outcome of their refugee applications. Some 1,400 East Timorese, who arrived since 1994, live on visitor visas waiting a court ruling on their status.
Australia has witnessed a record number of complaints of racial discrimination in recent months as a four-month long race debate brought latent xenophobia into the open.
The latest reports of racial abuse came from Malaysians studying in Australia, who say they have been verbally assaulted and spat at.
According to Royal Melbourne Institute of Technology the overseas image of Australian universities and of the community in general was one of bigotry and racism.

The Institute's student union president Cecilia Leung said racism had always existed on Australian campuses, but that it had worsened since September when maverick politican Pauline Hanson claimed Australia was being swamped by Asians.
Asians make up 4.7 percent of the 18 million population and about one third of the annual 100,000 migrants.
"There is no doubt that things have got worse since she started speaking out about Asians and Aborigines," Leung said.
"In the past there were a lot of people who kept their views to themselves, but it seems that Pauline Hanson has given them the licence to air their views and to hurt people," she said.

In his pre-Christmas message, Sydney's Anglican Archbishop Harry Goodhew called for compassion for those in need, adding that Christmas in Australia was becoming a time of animosity, self-interest and greed. The Anglican church is Australia's second largest denomination after the Roman Catholic Church.
Goodhew said Australia had become a divided society, with the rich getting richer and the poor poorer.
He said a rising tide of gambling, domestic violence and drug abuse was afflicting Australian families, adding that 14 percent of Australian children live in poverty.
"Christmas, the traditional time of peace and goodwill to all, in Australia is rapidly becoming a time of animosity, self-interest and greed," Goodhew said.
"Fewer Australians are willing to help those in need," he said. "Sadly, the 25 to 34 year-olds have been found to be the least altruistic and most materially ambitious generation."
